paper_b.title: Dirac's theorem on chordal graphs implies Brooks' theorem

metadata.description: Both papers reprove Brooks' theorem (and its list-coloring strengthening) using fundamentally different machinery. Paper A uses the Alon-Tarsi algebraic / Eulerian-subgraph-parity method, supported by a structural lemma producing an induced even cycle with at most one chord. Paper B uses Dirac's theorem on chordal graphs together with a minimum-counterexample / chordless-cycle surgery argument. The shared theorem statements (Brooks; list-Brooks) align cleanly, but the supporting lemmas, definitions, and proof steps are largely paper-specific.

matches.explanation: Both nodes are Brooks' Theorem (1941), cited as the same external classical result. Paper A states it for connected $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$, excluding odd cycles and complete graphs; paper B states it for $\Delta \geq 3$ excluding $K_{\Delta+1}$ (the $\Delta=2$ odd-cycle case is dropped because the hypothesis $\Delta \geq 3$ rules it out). Same theorem up to phrasing of the exceptions.

Both are the list-coloring strengthening of Brooks' theorem: a connected graph $G \neq K_{\Delta+1}$ (and not an odd cycle, in paper A) with maximum degree $\Delta$ is list $\Delta$-colorable. Paper A states it as a corollary of its main result (with paintability added); paper B states it as Theorem 1, attributing it to Vizing / Erdős-Rubin-Taylor. Same mathematical statement on the list-coloring side.

Paper A's main theorem (list degree colorability + degree paintability for non-Gallai-tree connected graphs) is strictly stronger than paper B's list-Brooks (it allows lists of size $\deg(v)$ rather than $\Delta$, and adds the on-line / paintability version). Both papers' main contribution is a re-proof of a Brooks-type list-coloring statement, but paper A's framing via Gallai trees and paintability is a generalization beyond paper B's Theorem 1.

These are the two papers' main proofs of Brooks-type list-coloring results. They share zero machinery: paper A's proof builds an orientation and counts even/odd Eulerian subgraphs (Alon-Tarsi route); paper B's proof takes a minimum counterexample, uses Dirac's theorem to force a chordless cycle, and performs the $F$/$H$ surgery + greedy extension along the cycle. Same target theorem, fundamentally different proof technique — the canonical 'AP' alignment of the pair.

Both proofs invoke a structural fact extracting a special induced cycle from a graph that fails the relevant exceptional structure. Paper A's Lemma 1 produces an induced *even* cycle with at most one chord in any non-Gallai-tree connected graph — a substantial result proved in five claims. Paper B's analogue is the immediate observation (PSP431.4 + PSP431.5) that a non-chordal graph contains a chordless cycle of length $\geq 4$ — a one-line consequence of the definition of chordal. They serve the same structural role (extract a usable cycle from a non-exceptional graph) but the depth and form differ markedly.

Both papers introduce a vertex ordering whose purpose is to sequentialize the coloring/argument. Paper A's DFS-ordering lemma yields an ordering where every non-root vertex follows a neighbor (used to control Eulerian-subgraph orientation). Paper B uses Dirac's theorem to obtain a perfect elimination ordering on chordal graphs, where each vertex's earlier neighbors form a clique. Conceptual role is similar (orderings enabling step-by-step reasoning), but the orderings themselves and the properties they guarantee are quite different.

Both are short proofs that an ordering / greedy argument works: paper A proves the DFS ordering exists via a rooted spanning tree; paper B proves Lemma 1 by greedy coloring along a perfect elimination ordering. The mechanics differ (existence-of-ordering vs greedy-along-ordering), but both pivot on the 'order plus local property' technique. Low-confidence pairing offered as a soft analogy.
The Alon-Tarsi theorem (cited external result driving paper A's algebraic method) has no counterpart in paper B, which avoids the algebraic / polynomial-method framework entirely.
Schauz's paintability strengthening of Alon-Tarsi (the on-line / Paint-Correct game version) is specific to paper A's machinery; paper B does not consider paintability.
'Even Eulerian subgraph' is intrinsic to the Alon-Tarsi method and absent from paper B's chordal-graph framework.
'Odd Eulerian subgraph' has no analogue in paper B for the same reason as DP409.1.
$(k+1)$-paintability via the Paint-Correct game is paper-A-specific; paper B does not treat on-line / paintability versions of Brooks.

The notion of a Gallai tree (blocks are complete graphs or odd cycles) is the structural concept paper A excludes to characterize the non-exceptional case. Paper B uses 'connected and not $K_{\Delta+1}$' instead and never invokes Gallai trees.

'List degree colorable' (lists of size $\deg(v)$) is the strengthened property paper A's main theorem delivers. Paper B only treats the weaker $\Delta$-list version, so this finer notion has no node-level counterpart in paper B.
'Degree paintable' is the on-line / paintability sharpening; paper B has no paintability content.
Paper B explicitly defines a (proper) $k$-coloring; paper A treats this as background and never introduces an explicit definition node for it.
Paper B explicitly defines 'list assignment' as a node; paper A uses lists $L(v)$ implicitly inside theorem statements without a dedicated definition node.
Paper B's '$L$-colorable' definition has no separate definition node in paper A (which uses the concept implicitly).
'Chordal graph' is central to paper B but not used in paper A; paper A's structural framework uses Gallai trees instead.

Paper B's Lemma 1 (chordal graphs are list-colorable from lists of size $\omega$) is the engine of its proof. Paper A's machinery (Alon-Tarsi + structural lemma on Gallai trees) does not contain this chordal-graph result.

Paper A's proof of its structural lemma (the five-claim argument bounding chords and parity of the shortest non-Gallai-witnessing cycle) is a self-contained combinatorial argument with no analogue in paper B, which never proves a comparable structural statement.

Claim 1 of paper A (existence of a cycle in a non-Gallai-tree graph that induces neither a complete graph nor an odd cycle) is internal scaffolding of paper A's structural lemma; paper B never reasons about such cycles.
Claim 2 (no universal vertex on the shortest such cycle of length $\geq 5$) is paper-A-internal; paper B has nothing parallel.
Claim 3 (each vertex of the shortest such cycle is incident to at most one chord) is paper-A-internal scaffolding of the structural lemma's proof.
Claim 4 (the shortest such cycle is even) is paper-A-internal.
Claim 5 (the shortest such cycle has at most one chord total) is paper-A-internal.
